title: Browser History

concept.title: An array with a current position and an end
body: A browser keeps the pages you visited. `back` goes to an earlier page, `forward` to a page you went back from, and `visit url` opens a new page and **throws away all pages that were "forward"** from the current one. Two stacks work, but a simpler way is an **array** with two numbers: `cur`, the index of the current page, and `end`, the index of the last page that you can still reach with `forward`.

body.code:
visit u:   cur += 1; pages[cur] = u; end = cur        # the old forward pages are forgotten
back k:    cur = max(0, cur - k)
forward k: cur = min(end, cur + k)

body: `visit` writes over the old page at `cur + 1` and moves `end` to the new position, which forgets everything after it without deleting anything. Using one array with `cur` and `end` makes every operation O(1) (`back` and `forward` move in one step, however large `k` is).

statement: A browser starts on the page `home`. Process `n` operations. `visit url` goes to a new page; all pages that you could reach with `forward` are forgotten. `back k` goes back by `k` pages, but at most to the first page. `forward k` goes forward by `k` pages, but at most to the last page that can be reached. After every operation print the current page.
inputFormat: The first line has the page `home`.
Each of the next `n` lines has an operation and a word: `visit url`, `back k` or `forward k`.
outputFormat: One line with the current page after each operation.
constraints: Page names are words of 1 to 10 lowercase letters.

examples.note: a, b, a (back), b (forward), c (new page), c (nothing to go forward to).

hints: Keep an array of pages, the index `cur` of the current page and the index `end` of the last reachable page.
`visit` writes the new page at `cur + 1` and sets `end = cur + 1`.
`back` and `forward` only change `cur`, within the limits 0 and `end`.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

home = input().strip()
n = int(input())
ops = [input().split() for _ in range(n)]

# Your code here

explanation: One array with the current index and the last reachable index describes the whole history. `visit` overwrites the next slot and shortens the forward part, `back` and `forward` clamp the index.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

home = input().strip()
n = int(input())
ops = [input().split() for _ in range(n)]

pages = [""] * (n + 1)
pages[0] = home
cur = 0
end = 0
out = []
for op, val in ops:
    if op == "visit":
        cur += 1
        pages[cur] = val
        end = cur
    elif op == "back":
        cur = max(0, cur - int(val))
    else:
        cur = min(end, cur + int(val))
    out.append(pages[cur])
print("\n".join(out))
